title: See & Spray targeted applications reduce herbicide use while maintaining at least 93% weed control in soybean trials
summary: Targeted sprays matched broadcast weed control within 1% in four U.S. site-years. The Results report herbicide savings of 62.4% before emergence and 28.4% and 36.5% after emergence.
account: University of Arkansas weed scientists and Blue River Technology agronomists ran four site-years of randomized complete block trials in 2021 and 2022. Sites were the Northeast Research and Extension Center in Keiser, Arkansas, and Stoneville R&D in Greenville, Mississippi. They compared John Deere See & Spray machine-vision targeted applications with traditional broadcast programs in glyphosate/glufosinate/dicamba-resistant soybean. They used a preemergence residual followed by early-postemergence dicamba and mid-postemergence glufosinate. Targeted applications gave control comparable to broadcast, with at most 1% less efficacy. Overall control was 93% or more for Palmer amaranth, broadleaf signalgrass, morningglory and purslane species. Soybean injury fell by at most 5 percentage points without a yield increase. The Results assign mean savings of 62.4% to preemergence, 28.4% to early-postemergence, and 36.5% to mid-postemergence applications, with narrower nozzle angles spraying less area. The paper appeared online on 15 November 2024. It is a research trial, not a commercial farm deployment.
purpose: Detect weeds with machine vision and apply herbicide only where weeds are present, reducing herbicide use while maintaining control.
system: John Deere See & Spray (machine-vision targeted sprayer)
model_version: See & Spray model year 2022 (level 3 detection sensitivity, small coverage buffer)
deployer: University of Arkansas and Stoneville R&D field trials (Keiser, AR and Greenville, MS)
taxonomy_note: Herbicide saved is read as reduced waste; it is also a cost saving for the grower.

ratings.reason: Savings of 28.4–62.4% on postemergence herbicide were measured in trial plots. No grower's costs or outcomes are documented.
Reduced herbicide volume is a trial result. No environmental outcome off-plot is measured.

ai_role.statement: The machine-vision sprayer decided where to spray. The comparison with broadcast programs is a randomized trial with consistent herbicides and rates. Savings depended on nozzle angle and machine settings. Co-authored by the maker's agronomists with university weed scientists.

evidence.citation: Avent TH, Norsworthy JK, Patzoldt WL, Schwartz-Lazaro LM, Houston MM, Butts TR, Vazquez AR. Comparing herbicide application methods with See & Spray technology in soybean. Weed Technology 38:e74 (2024). doi:10.1017/wet.2024.70

headline: See & Spray reduces herbicide use in soybean trials

comparator.against: traditional broadcast herbicide applications in the same randomized trials
comparator.before: full broadcast applications of the postemergence herbicides (traditional broadcast program)
comparator.after: Targeted applications saved 28.4% in early-postemergence and 36.5% in mid-postemergence treatments, with comparable weed control
comparator.quote: On average, targeted sprays saved a range of 28.4% to 62.4% on postemergence herbicides. On the basis of these results, with specific machine settings, targeted application programs could reduce the amount of herbicide applied while providing weed control comparable to that of traditional broadcast applications.

later.note: John Deere reported that customers ran See & Spray on more than five million acres in the 2025 season, cutting non-residual herbicide use by nearly half.
later.quote: John Deere’s See & Spray technology was used across more than five million acres of farmland during the 2025 growing season – a land area larger than the state of New Jersey. In 2025, John Deere customers reduced non-residual herbicide use by an average of nearly 50% — saving nearly 31 million gallons of herbicide mix—demonstrating the power of targeted application, even in a season marked by elevated weed pressure and frequent rains.

fields.account: University of Arkansas weed scientists and Blue River Technology agronomists ran four site-years of randomized complete block trials in 2021 and 2022. Sites were the Northeast Research and Extension Center in Keiser, Arkansas, and Stoneville R&D in Greenville, Mississippi. They compared John Deere See & Spray machine-vision targeted applications with traditional broadcast programs in glyphosate/glufosinate/dicamba-resistant soybean. They used a preemergence residual followed by early-postemergence dicamba and mid-postemergence glufosinate. Targeted applications gave control comparable to broadcast, with at most 1% less efficacy. Overall control was 93% or more for Palmer amaranth, broadleaf signalgrass, morningglory and purslane species. Soybean injury fell by at most 5 percentage points without a yield increase. The Results assign mean savings of 62.4% to preemergence, 28.4% to early-postemergence, and 36.5% to mid-postemergence applications, with narrower nozzle angles spraying less area. The paper appeared online on 15 November 2024. It is a research trial, not a commercial farm deployment.
